title: Luck or cause: when two things happen together, what does it show?

summary.text: On a hot beach in Kerala, the more ice golas a cart sold in a day, the more people went home sunburnt. Do golas burn skin? Your child will flip a coin 200 times to see how often luck alone makes a pattern, and measure okra pods to see what a pattern can and cannot tell us. Then they learn four ways to test a pattern fairly: look for a hidden third thing, compare with a group that did not get the thing, let a coin choose the groups, and hide who got what. They also meet John Snow, the doctor who used a map and a comparison to find out what was really making people ill in London in 1854.
summary.art: A busy beach with a red-and-orange ice gola cart in the shade, a hot yellow sun above it, and several people with red shoulders walking away eating golas.

intro.hook: On a Kerala beach, a doctor counted the people who came to her tent with sunburn each day. A gola seller counted the golas he sold. On the days he sold more golas, she saw more sunburn. A man in the crowd said, "Ban the golas!" Was he right?
intro.text: The two counts really did rise and fall together. That was true. But the idea that golas burn skin may still be wrong. You may already know three questions to ask about any claim: says who, how do they know, who is missing. This time you ask a harder question. When two things go together, what is really going on? You will use a coin, okra pods and some sweet cups to find out.
intro.art: A doctor's tent on a beach with two tally charts pinned up side by side, one headed Golas sold and the other Sunburn cases, and a gola cart in the background.

outcomes: I can explain why two things happening together does not show that one causes the other.
I can look for a hidden third thing behind a pattern, and check it by comparing like with like.
I can say why a few tries can look special by chance, and why more tries give better evidence.
I can explain why a fair comparison needs a control group, and why a coin should choose the groups.
I can explain what a blind test and a placebo are, and why they are used.
I can spot sneaky tricks in evidence: only the hits, too few tries, asking only fans, and a seller testing their own product.
I can tell how John Snow used a map and a comparison in 1854 to show what was making people ill.

terms.meaning: Two things that rise and fall together. When one goes up, the other tends to go up too.
terms.example: On a beach, more golas were sold on the days when more people got sunburnt.
terms.art: Two lines on a graph that both climb up together from left to right.

terms.meaning: Something that makes another thing happen. If you take the cause away, the result goes away too.
terms.example: Pressing the switch makes the fan turn. Cut the power and the fan stops.
terms.art: A finger pressing a wall switch with an arrow to a spinning ceiling fan.

terms.meaning: Something that is not in your table but makes two things in the table rise and fall together. Scientists call it a confounder.
terms.example: Hot sunshine makes people buy golas and also makes them sunburnt. The sun is the hidden third thing.
terms.art: A bright sun with two arrows pointing down, one to a gola and one to a red-shouldered person.

terms.meaning: What happens when nothing pushes the result one way or the other, like a coin landing heads or tails. Chance can still make patterns.
terms.example: A coin can land heads four times in a row with no help from anybody.
terms.art: A coin spinning in the air above a steel plate.

terms.meaning: The same result coming up several times in a row.
terms.example: Heads, heads, heads, heads is a streak of four.
terms.art: A row of five coins on a table, all showing heads.

terms.meaning: One go at a test. One coin flip is one trial. Ten flips are ten trials.
terms.example: A child who flips a coin 200 times has done 200 trials.
terms.art: A child's hand flipping a coin with a tally of strokes beside it.

terms.meaning: How much the results jump around from one set of tries to the next. With few trials the spread is big. With many trials the results settle.
terms.example: Ten flips can give 3 heads or 8 heads. Two hundred flips will give close to 100 heads.
terms.art: Two dot charts, one with dots scattered widely and one with dots close together.

terms.meaning: The group that is treated the same as the others, except that it does not get the thing being tested. You compare the test group with it.
terms.example: One banana is wrapped at the stalk. Its twin from the same bunch is left bare. The bare banana is the control.
terms.art: Two bananas from the same bunch on a plate, one with foil on the stalk and one without.

terms.meaning: Decided by chance, with nobody choosing. A coin flip is a fair way to be random.
terms.example: A coin flip decides which of two cups gets the fancy label.
terms.art: A coin held above two paper cups.

terms.meaning: A test where the people being tested do not know which group they are in. In a double-blind test the people measuring do not know either.
terms.example: Tasting two cups without knowing which one has the fancy label.
terms.art: A girl with a scarf over her eyes holding out a hand to take a paper cup.

terms.meaning: A dummy treatment with nothing active in it, such as a sugar pill. It lets a test separate the effect of the real treatment from the effect of expecting to feel better.
terms.example: In a medicine test, one group gets the medicine and another gets a plain sugar pill that looks the same.
terms.art: Two identical white pills on a spoon, one marked with a small star on the back.

terms.meaning: Showing only the results that fit your story and hiding the rest, like picking only the best cherries from a basket.
terms.example: A shop shows three happy customers and does not mention the thirty who sent the product back.
terms.art: A hand picking red cherries from the top of a basket while ripe-looking and spoiled ones sit hidden below.

terms.meaning: One person's story about what happened to them. It can be true and still not show what caused it.
terms.example: "My cousin drank this tea and his cold went away" is an anecdote.
terms.art: A speech bubble over a man holding a cup of tea.

terms.meaning: When the person doing a test would gain if the answer comes out one way, for example because they sell the product.
terms.example: A biscuit company says its own tests show its biscuits make children cleverer.
terms.art: A man in a company coat holding a biscuit box and a clipboard that says RESULTS.

terms.meaning: A real-life situation where luck has already made two groups that differ in only one way, so we can compare them without setting up a test.
terms.example: Two water companies supplying the same streets, so neighbours drank different water.
terms.art: A street with houses on both sides, some with a blue pipe and some with a green pipe.

terms.meaning: A serious illness of the gut, caused by a bacterium called Vibrio cholerae. Cholera spreads when people drink water or eat food that carries the bacterium.
terms.example: Clean boiled drinking water helps stop cholera from spreading.
terms.art: A glass of clear water beside a steel pot of boiling water.

explanations.concept: Two things that go together: what a pattern can and cannot show
explanations.definition: A correlation means two things rise and fall together. It is a real pattern, but it does not show that one thing causes the other.
explanations.description: On a beach in May, the more golas the cart sold, the more people got sunburnt. The numbers really did go together. That is called a correlation. A correlation is worth noticing, because it tells you where to look. But it does not tell you what is making what happen. To know that, you have to do more work. You can look for a third thing, check which came first, and compare with a situation where one of the two is missing.
examples: More golas sold and more sunburn on the same days is a correlation.
Taller children read better books. Height does not help reading. Both come with being older.
On the days more umbrellas are open in Chennai, the roads are wetter. Neither makes the other happen. Rain is behind both.
explanations.art: A scatter of dots on a graph climbing from bottom left to top right, labelled Golas sold and Sunburn cases.
explanations.context: This card explains what a correlation is, and why it is only the start of an answer.

explanations.definition: A hidden third thing is something outside your table that pushes two things in the table up and down together. Scientists call it a confounder.
explanations.description: Ask: what else is different on the days when both numbers are high? On the beach the answer is the hot sun. Sun makes people buy golas, and sun burns skin. The golas and the sunburn never touched each other. To check, compare like with like. Look only at sunny days, so the sun is the same in every row. If golas still go with sunburn when the sun is the same, golas might matter. If they do not, the sun was doing it all.
examples: Fire engines and damage: the bigger the fire, the more engines come and the more damage there is. The size of the fire is the hidden third thing.
Children with big shoes spell better. Age is behind both.
Towns with more tea stalls have more phone shops. The size of the town is behind both.
explanations.art: The sun in the middle with one arrow down to a gola and one to a sunburnt shoulder, and a dotted line with a cross between the gola and the shoulder.
explanations.context: This card explains what a hidden third thing is and how to check for one.

explanations.concept: Which way round? Sometimes the arrow points the other way
explanations.definition: Sometimes two things go together because the second one causes the first. If you draw an arrow from the cause to the result, it points the opposite way from what you guessed.
explanations.description: Children who go to the dentist many times have more fillings. Does the dentist cause fillings? No. Having bad teeth sends children to the dentist. The cause comes first, and the visit follows. Whenever two things go together, ask which one came first, and ask whether the second one might be causing the first. A diary, a photo with a date, or a timestamped record can show which came first.
examples: People who carry inhalers have more breathing trouble. The trouble is why they carry them.
Wet umbrellas outside the school door do not cause rain. Rain causes wet umbrellas.
Where there are more doctors, more people seem ill. Illness brings doctors to a place.
explanations.art: A child in a dentist's chair with two arrows: a crossed-out one from dentist to fillings and a ticked one from sore teeth to dentist.
explanations.context: This card explains another thing to check when two things go together: which one came first.

explanations.definition: Chance means no cause is pushing the result. Even so, chance makes streaks and lumps that look like patterns, most often when you have only a few tries.
explanations.description: A fair coin lands heads about half the time. In ten flips, though, you will often see 7 heads, because ten flips is a small number. About one set in every six sets of ten flips shows 7 or more heads, by luck alone. In a long run of flips, a streak of four heads in a row turns up many times. People who see a streak often feel a reason must be behind it. Usually the reason is just luck. The way to tell is to ask how often chance alone would do that.
examples: Your cricket team wins three matches in a row when you wear a red shirt. Three is a small number.
Two buses to the same stop come together. Chance bunches things up.
A fair coin gives five heads in a row once in a while. It is not broken.
explanations.art: A strip of twenty coins in a row with a bracket under four heads in a row, labelled luck.
explanations.context: This card explains why luck alone can look like a pattern, as the 200 coin flips in The Lucky Coin experiment show.

explanations.definition: The more times you try something, the closer the results get to what usually happens. With few tries, the results jump around.
explanations.description: In ten flips, the number of heads can swing from 3 to 8. In 100 flips, the number of heads is between 40 and 60 about 96 times out of 100. In 200 flips, it stays even closer to half. So 7 heads out of 10 is not strong evidence of anything. But 70 heads out of 100 would be, because chance almost never does that. This does not mean bigger is always better. If a test is unfair, asking more of the same people only gives you more of the wrong answer.
examples: A bowler who takes 3 wickets in one match may be lucky. One who takes 3 wickets a match for 40 matches is good.
Tasting one spoonful from a jar tells you little about the whole jar. Ten spoonfuls from different places in the jar tell you more.
In 1936 a US magazine got more than two million replies to its poll and still guessed the wrong winner. It had asked the wrong people.
explanations.art: Two bar charts side by side: one made from 10 flips with uneven bars, and one made from 200 flips with bars close to the middle.
explanations.context: This card explains why a few tries are shaky evidence and why many tries are steadier.

explanations.concept: A fair comparison needs a control group
explanations.definition: A control group is treated exactly like the test group, except for the one thing being tested. The only way to see what a thing does is to compare it with a case where it is missing.
explanations.description: Suppose someone says wrapping the stalk of a banana slows its ripening. If you wrap one banana and watch it, you learn nothing, because bananas ripen anyway. You need a second banana, from the same bunch, kept in the same place, with no wrapping. That is the control. If the wrapped banana ripens slower, the wrapping might be the reason. Then you check by trying again. It is like checking the old saying that a crow's call means guests are coming: you also need to look at the days when no crow called. A control group is that idea, made on purpose.
examples: A medicine test gives the medicine to one group and a dummy pill to another.
A new fertiliser is tried on half the pots, while the other half get plain water.
A school tries a new reading method in one class and keeps another class on the old way.
explanations.art: Two pots of the same plant side by side, one labelled Test and one labelled Control, in the same sunny window.
explanations.context: This card explains why you need a control group to see what any treatment really does.

explanations.concept: Let a coin choose the groups
explanations.definition: Random means chance decides who goes into which group. This stops the person running the test from choosing, even by accident, the ones who would do better.
explanations.description: Suppose you test a plant food on six plants. If you pick which plants get it, you may give it to the strongest ones without noticing. Then the strong plants grow more, and the food gets the credit. A coin flip has no favourites. Heads goes in group A. Tails goes in group B. Over many items, the two groups come out alike in every way except the thing you are testing. You may not know all the hidden third things, and a coin takes care of them anyway.
examples: Flip a coin to decide which of two cups gets the fancy label.
Draw names from a hat to decide who tries the new game first.
Flip a coin for each banana from the bunch to decide which one is wrapped.
explanations.art: A hand flipping a coin over six seedlings, with heads going to a left tray and tails to a right tray.
explanations.context: This card explains why a coin flip is a fair way to make two groups.

explanations.concept: Blind tests and the placebo effect
explanations.definition: In a blind test, people do not know which group they are in. A placebo is a dummy treatment. Both are used because expecting something can change how people feel.
explanations.description: In many medicine tests, people who were given a plain sugar pill said their pain was less, and some said they felt better. This is called the placebo effect. The feelings are real. The sugar pill did not kill germs or heal bones, though. If a test does not have a placebo group, the effect of expecting to feel better gets mixed up with the effect of the medicine. So testers do not tell people which pill they got. That is a blind test. In a double-blind test, the doctors giving out the pills do not know who got which either, so no sign, look or word can give it away.
examples: Two cups of the same water, one labelled expensive. Many people say the labelled one tastes better.
A new tablet is tested against a look-alike sugar tablet, and nobody knows who got which until the end.
A teacher marks maths papers with the names covered, so the child's name cannot change the mark.
explanations.art: Two identical white pills on a spoon with a curtain between a doctor and a patient.
explanations.context: This card explains blind tests and the placebo effect, and why testers use them.

explanations.definition: Evidence can mislead even when every number in it is true. Showing only the hits, too few tries, asking only fans, and tests run by sellers are the common tricks.
explanations.description: Here are five ways true numbers can mislead. One: only the hits are shown, like three happy customers out of three hundred. Two: too few tries, like a toothpaste tested on five people. Three: only the fans were asked, like a survey handed out at the biscuit stall. Four: the seller ran the test, so it might be tilted. Five: a chart that starts its bars at 90 instead of 0, so a tiny gap looks huge. None of these proves a claim is wrong. They tell you to ask for more before you believe it.
examples: "Nine out of ten users agree!" Nine out of ten of which ten people?
A bar chart where one bar looks twice as tall because the scale starts at 90.
A cereal box says a study found children who eat the cereal do better. The cereal company paid for the study.
explanations.art: Two bar charts of the same two numbers, one starting at zero with similar bars and one starting at 90 with a tiny bar and a tall bar.
explanations.context: This card lists five tricks that can make true numbers mislead, and what to ask about each.

explanations.concept: When you cannot run the test: a natural experiment
explanations.definition: A natural experiment is a real-world case where luck has already sorted people into two groups that differ in just one way. Scientists compare them as if they had set up the test.
explanations.description: In 1854 many people in one part of London were dying of cholera. Most doctors thought it spread through bad air. A doctor named John Snow had another idea: it spread through water. He could not run a test that gave half the people clean water and half dirty water. That would have been wrong. But he found streets where neighbours were supplied by two different water companies, one drawing water from a dirtier place on the river. The streets, the poverty and the air were the same. The only difference was the water. The households with the dirtier water had many times more deaths. This was strong evidence, and he had not run a test himself.
examples: Two villages get electricity in different years, and scientists compare their school results.
A new road splits a town, and doctors compare the health of the two sides.
Twins who grow up in different cities can be compared on one thing at a time.
explanations.art: A street of terrace houses with a blue pipe going to the left side and a green pipe going to the right side, and red crosses on mostly the blue houses.
explanations.context: This card explains how a doctor in 1854 found a cause without being able to run a test.

explanations.description: Not all evidence is equal. Here is one way to rank it, from weakest to strongest. A single story is weakest. A table of every case is better. A comparison with a control group is better again. A comparison where a coin chose the groups and nobody knew who got what is stronger still. The strongest evidence is many such tests, done by different people in different places, that agree. People still argue about how to rank evidence, and some questions can never be tested with an experiment, such as what happened in history or what is inside a star. For those, scientists use the best comparisons they can find.
examples: One person says the tea cured their cold. That is a single story.
A coin-chosen, blind test of the tea on 400 people is much stronger.
Ten such tests in ten countries that all agree is stronger again.
explanations.art: A ladder with five rungs labelled A story, A table of all cases, A control group, Random and blind, Many tests agree, with a child climbing it.
explanations.context: This card gives one way to rank evidence, and says honestly that people still argue about it.

explanations.concept: How strong must the evidence be?
explanations.description: How much evidence is enough? Thinkers disagree. One idea is that the stranger the claim, the stronger the evidence must be. Another is to start from how likely the claim seemed before you saw any evidence, and let each piece of evidence change your mind a little. Both agree that a story is not enough.
examples: A claim that the Moon is made of cheese needs much more than a claim that it will rain tomorrow.
A claim that a new vitamin helps people sleep is believable, but still needs a fair comparison.

perspectives.who: Carl Sagan, an American astronomer (1934 to 1996)
perspectives.explanation: Extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence. The odder the claim, the more you should ask for.

perspectives.who: Thinkers who use probability, sometimes called Bayesians
perspectives.explanation: Start with how likely the claim seemed before you saw any evidence. Each piece of evidence then makes you believe it a little more or a little less. Odd claims start out unlikely, so they need more evidence, but nothing is ruled out.
Use the same careful standard for every claim. Oddness is a reason to check twice, but the test is the same.

explanations.art: Three people at a see-saw, with a feather labelled Weather forecast on one side and a heavy stone labelled Moon is cheese on the other.
explanations.context: This card is about a question people still argue over: how strong must evidence be before a claim is accepted?

agreed.text: Two things going together does not show that one causes the other.
agreed.evidence: Again and again, a third thing has been found behind a pattern, such as the sun behind golas and sunburn. In London in 1854, the doctor John Snow found that water was spreading cholera by looking for what was behind a pattern of deaths.

agreed.text: Chance alone can make results that look special, especially with few tries.
agreed.evidence: With a fair coin, about one set of ten flips in six gives 7 or more heads. This follows from counting the ways a coin can fall, and the 200 flips in The Lucky Coin experiment show it.

agreed.text: To see what a thing does, compare with a group that did not get it.
agreed.evidence: Medicine tests, farm trials and school studies all use a control group, because without one the effect of the treatment cannot be told from things that would have happened anyway.

agreed.text: Expecting to feel better can change how people feel, so good tests use a placebo and do not tell people which group they are in.
agreed.evidence: In many tests, people given dummy pills reported less pain than people given nothing. A large review of such tests found this effect, mostly for pain and nausea (feeling sick), which only the person themselves can report.

agreed.text: Many tries give steadier results than few tries, but more tries cannot fix a test that asked the wrong people.
agreed.evidence: The more times a coin is flipped, the closer the share of heads gets to half. In 1936 a US magazine got more than two million replies to its poll and still guessed the wrong winner, because of who was asked.

agreed.text: People who would gain from a result are not the best ones to test it.
agreed.evidence: Reviews of many studies found that studies paid for by the maker of a product more often favoured that product than studies paid for by others.

challenging.claim: If two things go together, one of them must cause the other.
challenging.for: Sometimes it is true. Smoke and fire go together, and fire does cause smoke.
challenging.against: Golas and sunburn went together, and the sun was behind both. A pattern is a reason to look closer, not an answer.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that a pattern always means a cause.

challenging.claim: What happened to me is the best proof.
challenging.for: Your own experience is real, and you saw it with your own eyes.
challenging.against: One person's story cannot say what would have happened without the treatment. Colds go away, and luck happens. Your story is a good reason to test, not the test itself.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that your own experience is enough to show a cause.

challenging.claim: If a poll or test has many people, it must be right.
challenging.who: Some people who like big numbers
challenging.for: More tries do give steadier results when the test is fair.
challenging.against: In 1936, a US magazine asked millions of people and still guessed wrong, because the people it asked were not like all voters. Asking a huge number of the wrong people still gives the wrong answer.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that a big number of people makes a test right.

challenging.claim: A placebo effect means the person was only imagining it.
challenging.for: A placebo has no active ingredient.
challenging.against: People in these tests report real changes, especially in pain, and some body measures change too. The feeling is real. But a sugar pill cannot kill germs or heal a broken bone.
challenging.context: This card is about what the placebo effect does and does not mean.

challenging.claim: We can only know a cause by running an experiment.
challenging.for: An experiment is the strongest way, because you set the groups yourself.
challenging.against: We cannot run experiments on stars, on history, or on things that would harm people. John Snow, a doctor in London in 1854, found the cause of cholera by comparing houses that luck had already sorted into two groups. Many scientists say careful comparisons are enough when experiments are impossible.
challenging.context: This card is about whether an experiment is the only way to find a cause.

big_questions.q: Golas and sunburn went together, but the sun was behind both. How many other things that we think are connected might really share a hidden third thing?
big_questions.hint: Think of two things you believe go together, and ask what else is different on those days.

big_questions.q: If chance makes streaks and patterns all the time, how can anyone tell a real pattern from a lucky one?
big_questions.hint: Think about how many times you would have to flip the coin to be sure.

big_questions.q: A sugar pill can make people feel less pain. What does that tell us about the link between what we expect and what our bodies do?
big_questions.hint: Think of how you feel when a grown-up kisses a bump.

big_questions.q: We cannot run an experiment on the Sun or on history. How can we ever know what caused what in such cases?
big_questions.hint: Think of John Snow, the doctor who compared houses on the same streets that got water from two different companies.

big_questions.q: Who should test a new product: the company that makes it, or someone else? And who should pay that someone else?
big_questions.hint: Think of a child marking their own homework.

big_questions.q: The philosopher David Hume said we never see a cause, only one thing following another many times. Do you agree?
big_questions.hint: Think about pushing a door. Do you see the push make it open, or do you just see push then open?

big_questions.q: A village farmer says her rain dance works because rain came the next day. Who should test it, and how would you do it kindly?
big_questions.hint: Think about the days she danced and no rain came, and the days it rained without a dance.

big_questions.q: A pattern can be true, and useful, and still not be a cause. When is it fine to act on a pattern anyway?
big_questions.hint: Think of carrying an umbrella when you see dark clouds.

story.title: The Ban on the Gola Cart
story.note: A made-up story. The science in it is real: two counts can rise and fall together because a third thing, here the sun, is behind both, and comparing only days when the third thing is the same shows this. Ice golas are shaved ice with syrup, sold on beaches across India.
text: Meenu was ten, and every evening in May she helped her uncle Basheer at his ice gola cart on Kozhikode beach. Her job was to turn the handle of the shaver. The ice went chhk, chhk, chhk, and fell into a heap as white as snow. Uncle poured red syrup on it, then orange. People paid five rupees and walked away with a cold, sweet, dripping cone.

That week a green tent went up next to the cart. A banner said BEACH HEALTH CAMP. Inside sat Dr. Leela, who had a stethoscope round her neck and a big register in front of her. All day, people with red, burning shoulders came in. She wrote each one down.

On Sunday evening, the town councillor, Mrs. Fathima Beevi, came to the tent. A young man from the camp, Sreejith, pinned a sheet of paper to the board. On it was a table of seven days. One column said how many golas Uncle Basheer had sold, because Uncle always counted in his notebook. The next column said how many sunburn cases Dr. Leela had seen.
"Look," said Sreejith. "Big gola days are big sunburn days. Small gola days are small sunburn days." He tapped the board. "The golas are doing this."
Mrs. Fathima frowned. "Then golas must go. No carts on the beach from next Monday."

Uncle Basheer went very quiet. The cart had been his father's. Meenu looked at the paper. The numbers were true. She had seen them in Uncle's notebook herself. But something bothered her, and she could not say what.
At school, Mrs. Sulochana, her teacher, had a saying. "When two things go together, look for who else is standing there." Meenu copied the table into her own notebook.

She went through Uncle's pages with her friend Aysha. She added a new column on the right. Aysha had a good memory for the weather, so Meenu wrote it in: sunny, sunny, cloudy, sunny, cloudy, sunny, sunny.
"Look," whispered Aysha. "The two cloudy days are the two smallest days. Both columns."

Meenu put her finger on the Thursday row. The cart axle had broken on Thursday. Uncle had shut the cart all day. The golas column said zero. But the camp's column for Thursday said fourteen. Fourteen people had come in with sunburn on a day with no golas at all.
"That's odd," said Aysha. "If golas burn people, how did fourteen get burnt?"
Meenu thought hard. "Maybe the golas are not the thing. Maybe the sun is. Sun makes people want golas. Sun burns people. The golas and the burns never touch each other."
"But Sreejith will say you are only saying that to save your uncle," said Aysha.
Meenu nodded. "So I have to show it a way nobody can argue with. I can't just say the sun is behind it."

She thought for a long time, until the sky went dark. Then she took a clean page and wrote only the sunny days. Forty golas and thirteen burns. Thirty-eight golas and fifteen burns. Zero golas and fourteen burns. Ninety golas and fourteen burns. A hundred and twenty golas and fourteen burns.

"Now the sun is the same in every row," she told Aysha. "If golas made people burn, then on sunny days the big gola days would have more burns. Look. They don't. Forty or a hundred and twenty, it's about fourteen."
On Monday, Mrs. Fathima came back with Sreejith and Dr. Leela. Meenu stood in front of the tent with her chart paper. Her hands shook. She showed them the first table and the second.
"How do I know you are not just saying this for your uncle?" asked the councillor.
"You don't have to believe me," said Meenu. "Just look at the sunny days only. Then look at Thursday, when there were no golas at all."
Sreejith crossed his arms. "Five sunny days is not many. It could be luck."

Dr. Leela smiled. "He is right about that, and so is Meenu. Five days is few. Let's count for two more weeks. But Thursday is a good test. If golas caused the burns, a day without golas should have been quiet, and it was not. Meenu's idea could have failed that test, and it didn't."
Mrs. Fathima read the chart again, slowly. "So what does burn the skin?"
"The sun," said Meenu. "And standing in it for hours."
The councillor did not ban the carts. Instead she asked the camp to put up a shade tent, and to hand out caps. Dr. Leela asked Meenu to help her count for the next two weeks.
That evening Uncle Basheer filled a cone with red syrup and held it out to her. "The first one is yours," he said. "Cold, and sweet, and not guilty."
story.epiphany: Golas and sunburn rose and fell together because the hot sun was behind both. Meenu checked by looking only at the sunny days, so the sun was the same in every row, and the golas and the burns no longer went together. A day with no golas and plenty of burns also showed that golas were not the cause. A pattern tells you where to look. It does not tell you what is behind it.
ask: Why did Meenu add a column for the weather?
What did she see when she looked only at the sunny days?
Why was the Thursday with no golas such a good test?
Why did Dr. Leela say five sunny days was still few?
If golas were the cause, what would Meenu's table of only the sunny days have looked like?

games.title: Cause, Chance, Hidden Third Thing or Other Way Round? A card game
games.context: This is a card game about patterns. Each card names two things that go together. You decide what is really going on: does one cause the other, is it chance, is a hidden third thing behind both, or is it the other way round, with the second thing causing the first?

printables.title: 24 pattern cards: two things that go together on the front, the answer and the reason on the back

items.f: On days when more ice golas are sold, more people get sunburnt.
items.b: HIDDEN THIRD THING. Hot sun makes people buy golas and also burns skin. The golas never touch the burn.

items.f: The bigger a fire is, the more fire engines are sent. Big fires also have more damage. So engines and damage go together.
items.b: HIDDEN THIRD THING. The size of the fire is behind both. Engines do not cause the damage.

items.f: Children with bigger feet do better on spelling tests.
items.b: HIDDEN THIRD THING. Age is behind both. Older children have bigger feet and have also learned more spelling.

items.f: Towns with more tea stalls also have more mobile phone shops.
items.b: HIDDEN THIRD THING. The size of the town is behind both. Big towns have more of everything.

items.f: In months when more kulfi is sold, more ceiling fans are bought.
items.b: HIDDEN THIRD THING. Hot weather is behind both. Eating kulfi does not make anyone buy a fan.

items.f: Streets with more cars parked on them have more air conditioners fitted in the houses.
items.b: HIDDEN THIRD THING. How much money the families have is behind both. Cars do not switch on air conditioners.

items.f: Children who go to the dentist many times have more fillings.
items.b: OTHER WAY ROUND. Sore teeth send children to the dentist. The visits do not make the holes.

items.f: People who carry an inhaler have more trouble breathing.
items.b: OTHER WAY ROUND. The trouble with breathing is why they carry the inhaler.

items.f: Fields with more scarecrows have more crows.
items.b: OTHER WAY ROUND. A farmer puts up scarecrows because crows are coming. The crows came first.

items.f: In classes where the teacher shouts more, the children are noisier.
items.b: OTHER WAY ROUND. Noisy children make the teacher shout. It may also go the other way a little, but the noise usually comes first.

items.f: People who take more medicine are more ill.
items.b: OTHER WAY ROUND. Being ill is why they take the medicine.

items.f: Shops with more guards at the door have more thefts.
items.b: OTHER WAY ROUND. A shop that has many thefts hires more guards. The thefts came first.

items.f: Bean seeds kept damp in a jar sprout. The same kind of seeds kept dry do not.
items.b: CAUSE. This was tested. Only the water changed between the two jars, and the seeds with water sprouted.

items.f: Hands washed with soap have fewer germs than hands rinsed in plain water.
items.b: CAUSE. Scientists have counted germs from both kinds of hands. Soap lifts the germs off.

items.f: Potted plants on a windowsill lean towards the window.
items.b: CAUSE. Turn the pot round and the leaves slowly lean the other way, towards the light again.

items.f: In big tests where villages were chosen by chance, like a coin flip, children who slept under mosquito nets caught malaria less often.
items.b: CAUSE. Chance chose the villages, so the two groups were alike apart from the nets. This is a strong test.

items.f: A potato sinks in plain water and floats when enough salt is stirred in.
items.b: CAUSE. Only the salt changed, and the potato rose each time the salt was added.

items.f: Water in a pan with a lid comes to the boil sooner than water in an open pan.
items.b: CAUSE. A grown-up can test it with two equal pans. The lid keeps the heat in.

items.f: A girl wore her blue bangles to three matches, and her team won all three.
items.b: CHANCE. Three matches is too few to tell. Teams win some matches whatever anyone wears.

items.f: A fair coin came down heads five times in a row.
items.b: CHANCE. Streaks of five heads happen in a long run of flips with an ordinary coin.

items.f: Every time a man joins the shorter queue at the ration shop, the other queue moves faster.
items.b: CHANCE. It happens both ways, but we remember the annoying times and forget the lucky ones.

items.f: In a class of 30 children, two have the same birthday.
items.b: CHANCE. This is more likely than most people think. With 30 children, it happens about 7 times in 10.

items.f: A batter changes the grip of her bat and scores a fifty in the next three matches.
items.b: CHANCE, or too few matches to tell. A good player scores fifties sometimes. She would need many matches with each grip.

items.f: A girl wished for rain on a monsoon night, and it rained.
items.b: CHANCE. It rains on many monsoon nights, wishing or not.

Score sheet for up to 4 players

rules: Each player takes one token of each of the four kinds. Shuffle the 24 cards into a pile with the front side up.
The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not turn it over.
Everyone, the reader too, puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader turns the card and reads the answer and the reason. Each player with the right token scores one point.
Then each player who was right says in one sentence how they could check. A good check earns one more point.
Take turns to be the reader. The game ends when the pile is finished. The most points wins. If points are equal, you share the win.
Playing alone: pick a token for each card, then turn it over. Keep your score out of 24 and try to beat it next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the tokens. Give each player four tokens, one of each kind. Shuffle the cards and make a pile.
flow.say: Each card names two things that go together. You decide what is going on. One may cause the other. It may be chance. A hidden third thing may be behind both. Or it may be the other way round: the second thing causes the first.
flow.kid: Each card has two things that go together. Choose a token for what is really going on.
flow.context: This is the first step of the pattern card game. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Read the gola card first, as a practice. Let your child pick a token and give a reason before you turn the card.
flow.say: On days when more golas are sold, more people get sunburnt. What is really going on? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: More golas sold, more sunburn. What is really going on?

check.q: On days when more golas are sold on a beach, more people get sunburnt. What is the best explanation?
options: Golas make skin burn
Hot sun makes people buy golas and also burns skin
The sunburnt people were hungry
check.why: The hot sun is behind both. It makes people want cold golas and it burns their skin. A wrong pick usually means the pattern was taken for a cause.

flow.context: In this step, you play one practice card together.

flow.do: Play through the pile. Take turns to be the reader. After each card, ask each player how they could check their answer.
flow.say: Choose your token. Now everyone turn the tokens over together. I will read the answer. Who was right? How could we check?
flow.kid: Read a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Say how you could check.

ask.q: What question helped you most when you were not sure?
good: What else is different on those days?
Which one came first?
Could this happen by luck, with only a few tries?

flow.parent: Some cards are close calls. If your child gives a good reason for a different token, give the point and talk about it. The shouting-teacher card and the queue card can go two ways, and that is part of the lesson.
flow.context: In this step, you play the rest of the cards.

flow.do: Add up the points. Ask which card was the trickiest and which kind of pattern was easiest to spot.
flow.say: Which card was the trickiest? Which kind of pattern did you spot easily?
flow.kid: Which card was trickiest? Why?
flow.context: In this last step, you add up the points and talk about the hardest card.

games.title: Name the Trick: a card game about sneaky evidence
games.context: This is a game about adverts and claims that use true numbers in a misleading way. Each card gives one claim. You name the trick, and then say what you would ask to find out the truth.

printables.title: 18 trick cards: a claim on the front, the trick and the question to ask on the back

items.f: A toothpaste advert says: We tested our paste on 4 people, and all 4 said their teeth felt cleaner.
items.b: TOO FEW. Four people is a very small number. Chance alone can give four yes answers. Ask: how many people were tested, and were there more?

items.f: A runner took a new vitamin for two days and says he can run faster now.
items.b: TOO FEW. Two days is too short, and one runner is one try. Ask: how many runners, and for how long?

items.f: After one dry week, a shopkeeper says it never rains in his town these days.
items.b: TOO FEW. One week is a tiny sample of the weather. Ask: what do the rain records for many years say?

items.f: A fortune teller says: I told 3 people they would get good news, and all 3 did.
items.b: ONLY THE HITS. She does not say how many people she told. If she told a hundred, the three are the ones who remember her. Ask: how many did she tell in all?

items.f: A school website shows the five children who won prizes this year and says: Our children always win.
items.b: ONLY THE HITS. The hundreds of children who won nothing are not shown. Ask: how many children took part?

items.f: A gym shows photos of three members who lost weight. It does not say how many joined.
items.b: ONLY THE HITS. We see the successes and none of the others. Ask: out of everyone who joined, how many lost weight?

items.f: A survey outside a cricket stadium asks: Is cricket the best game? Everyone says yes.
items.b: ASKED ONLY FANS. People at a cricket match like cricket. Ask: who was left out?

items.f: An app asks only people who already use it whether it is easy to use. 9 out of 10 say yes.
items.b: ASKED ONLY FANS. People who found it hard have probably already given up and left. Ask: what do the people who stopped using it say?

items.f: A teacher asks only the children in the front row whether the lesson was clear.
items.b: ASKED ONLY FANS. The children at the back, who may find it harder to hear, were not asked. Ask: who is missing?

items.f: A juice company says: Our own test proves our juice makes children taller.
items.b: SELLER'S OWN TEST. The company gains if the answer is yes. Ask: who ran the test, and has someone else repeated it?

items.f: A shop says: We checked, and we have the best prices in town. They only looked at their own price list.
items.b: SELLER'S OWN TEST. They never compared with other shops. Ask: who did the comparing, and with what?

items.f: A tonic company pays a doctor to say on television that its tonic helps memory. No test is shown.
items.b: SELLER'S OWN TEST. The doctor is paid and no evidence is shown. Ask: where are the tests, and who paid for them?

items.f: A girl drank a herbal drink and her cough went away in four days. She says the drink cures coughs.
items.b: NO COMPARISON. Most coughs go away in a few days with no drink at all. Ask: what happens to people who do not drink it?

items.f: A farmer puts a new fertiliser on all his tomato plants and they grow big. He says the fertiliser did it.
items.b: NO COMPARISON. He has no plants left bare to compare with. Ask: how would they have grown without it?

items.f: A teacher plays music during a maths test and the marks go up. She says music raises marks. Last year's test was easier.
items.b: NO COMPARISON. She compared this year with last year, but the test changed too. Ask: what was different besides the music?

items.f: A cream advert says: It contains quantum-charged ionic particles that make skin glow. No test is shown.
items.b: SOUNDS SCIENTIFIC. Long science words are not evidence. Ask: what were the particles, and where is the test?

items.f: A bottle label says: Hexa-structured water raises focus by 300 percent. No study is named.
items.b: SOUNDS SCIENTIFIC. The number sounds exact but no one says how focus was measured. Ask: which study found this?

items.f: A packet says: 100 percent chemical-free.
items.b: SOUNDS SCIENTIFIC. Everything, including water and the packet itself, is made of chemicals. Ask: what does it really mean?

printables.title: 12 trick tokens: 2 each of TOO FEW, ONLY THE HITS, ASKED ONLY FANS, SELLER'S OWN TEST, NO COMPARISON, SOUNDS SCIENTIFIC

rules: Each player takes one trick token of each kind. With two players, use one set each. Shuffle the 18 cards into a pile.
The reader takes the top card and reads the claim aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Everyone puts down the token that names the trick. Turn the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. One point for each right token.
Then each player says what question they would ask. One more point for a good question.
Take turns to read. The game ends when all 18 cards are read. The most points wins, and equal scores share the win.
Playing alone: choose the token, turn the card, and score yourself out of 18.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Give each player a set of tokens. Read the six tricks aloud.
flow.say: Each card has a claim that uses true numbers in a sneaky way. There are six tricks. Your job is to name the trick.
flow.kid: Each card has a sneaky claim. Name the trick.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Name the Trick game. You set up the cards and the six tricks.

flow.do: Read the toothpaste card as a practice. Ask your child which trick it is and why before you turn the card.
flow.say: Four people were tested and all four said their teeth felt cleaner. Which trick is it? Why?
flow.kid: Four people tested a toothpaste. Which trick is it?

check.q: An advert says: We tested our paste on 4 people, and all 4 said their teeth felt cleaner. What is the main problem?
options: Four is too few, so chance alone could give this
Toothpaste cannot clean teeth
The people were not honest
check.why: With only four people, luck can easily make all four say yes. The paste may still be good, but this does not show it. A wrong pick usually means the child is looking for a lie, not a gap in the evidence.

flow.say: Choose the token that names the trick. Turn the tokens over together. Now say what you would ask.
flow.kid: Read the claim. Pick the trick. Say what you would ask.

ask.q: Which trick is the hardest to spot in a real advert?
good: Only the hits, because you do not see the people who are left out.
Sounds scientific, because long words sound clever.
No comparison, because the story seems to make sense.

experiments.title: The Lucky Coin: how often does chance alone look special?
experiments.context: In this experiment, you flip an ordinary coin 200 times, in 20 sets of 10, without wishing for heads or tails. You find out how often luck alone gives a result that looks special, such as 7 heads out of 10.
experiments.question: A friend says she can make heads come up by wishing, and she got 7 heads in 10 flips. How often does an ordinary coin, with no wishing, give 7 or more heads in 10 flips?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Out of 20 sets of 10 flips, how many sets will show 7 or more heads? Will your coin ever show 3 or fewer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same coin and toss it from the same height onto the same plate every time. Nobody wishes for heads, and nobody tries any tricks. Each set is exactly 10 flips, and heads is always the side with the picture on it. We write down every set, even the boring ones, and we do not throw away a set because it looks odd. Only chance decides the result.
results_table: 7 or more heads, or 3 or fewer?

materials.item: an ordinary coin (a one-rupee or two-rupee coin works)
a steel plate or tray with a folded cloth under it, so the coin does not roll away or clatter
a notebook and a pencil
a ruler, to draw the table with 20 rows
a second person to write down the results while your child flips

experiments.safety: Keep coins away from children under five, who might put them in their mouths.

schedule.what: Draw the table, flip 20 sets of 10, count, and compare with the friend's claim that she can make heads come up by wishing.

experiments.record: Fill in 20 rows, one for each set of 10 flips. Then count how many sets had 7 or more heads, and how many had 3 or fewer. Add up all the heads in the 200 flips. Last, draw a bar chart: one bar for each number of heads, from 0 to 10, showing how many sets had that number.

flow.do: Tell the story of the friend who got 7 heads in 10 flips. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both at the top of the page.
flow.say: A friend flipped a coin ten times and got seven heads. She says she wished it. If an ordinary coin is flipped ten times, how often do you think it gives seven or more heads? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A friend got 7 heads in 10 flips. Is that special? What do you guess? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think an ordinary coin will, or will not, give 7 heads sometimes?
good: It should give 5 heads each time, so 7 is odd.
It is a coin, so any number can come.
It is random, so sometimes 7 will come.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children think 5 heads should come every time. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Lucky Coin. You guess before you flip.

flow.do: Help your child draw a table with 20 rows and the four columns. Put the plate on a cloth. Practise two flips from about 20 centimetres above the plate.
flow.say: We flip the same way every time. Hold the coin about this high above the plate and let it drop. Heads is the side with the picture.
flow.kid: Draw the table. Flip from the same height onto the plate. Heads is the picture side.

check.q: Why must every flip be done in the same way, from the same height onto the same plate?
options: So the coin only lands the way chance decides
So the flips go faster
So the coin stays shiny
check.why: If you flip differently each time, how you flip might change the result. Then you could not say that chance alone made the pattern. A wrong pick usually means the child has not yet seen why one thing must stay the same.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the table and practise the flip.

flow.do: Your child flips 10 times for the first set. The helper tallies heads in a notebook. Do the next set and the next, up to 20 sets. Swap the flipper after every 5 sets.
flow.say: Flip ten times. I will count the heads. Do not wish for anything. Now the next set.
flow.kid: Flip 10 times. Your helper counts heads. Then do the next set. No wishing.
flow.wait: The 20 sets take about 15 minutes. Take a short break after set 10.
flow.parent: Stay calm about odd sets. If your child gets 8 heads or 2 heads in a set, say nothing and write it down. Also write the longest streak in each set, for example HHHH is a streak of four. If the coin rolls off the plate, repeat that flip.
flow.context: In this step, you flip the coin 200 times, in 20 sets of 10.

flow.do: Count the sets with 7 or more heads. Count the sets with 3 or fewer. Find the longest streak in all 20 sets. Write these three numbers under the table.
flow.say: How many sets had seven or more heads? How many had three or fewer? What is the longest streak you found?
flow.kid: Count the sets with 7 or more heads. Count the sets with 3 or fewer. Find the longest streak.

ask.q: Did the coin change in the sets that had many heads? What do you think made those sets happen?
good: No. It is the same coin. It was just luck.
I wished nothing, and it still happened.
Maybe ten flips is too few.

flow.parent: Most families find that 2 to 5 of the 20 sets show 7 or more heads. The exact number varies. If you got none, or ten, write it down and talk about it. Results that jump around like this are called the spread.
flow.context: In this step, you count how many sets looked special.

flow.do: Add up the heads from all 20 sets. Compare the total with 100, which is half of 200. Then compare it with the set that had the most heads.
flow.say: Add all the heads. Is it close to one hundred? The set with the most heads was far from five out of ten. Is the total of all 200 flips closer to half?
flow.kid: Add all your heads. Is the total close to 100? Is it closer to half than the set with the most heads?

check.q: One set of 10 flips gave 8 heads. All 200 flips together gave 103 heads. Why is the total closer to half?
options: Because more flips smooth out the luck of each set
Because the coin got tired
Because the last sets were easier
check.why: In a small set, luck can swing far from half. Over many flips, the highs and lows cancel out and the total settles near half. A wrong pick usually means the child thinks the coin itself changed.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the total of all flips with the single odd sets.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what the friend's 7 heads in 10 does and does not show. Ask for a claim, the evidence from the table, and the reasoning.
flow.say: Now think about your friend. What is your claim about her seven heads? What in your table is the evidence? What is your reason?
flow.kid: Does 7 heads in 10 show your friend can make heads come up by wishing? What is your evidence?

ask.q: What would the friend have to do to show she can really make heads come up by wishing?
good: Flip many more times and get far more than half heads.
Flip with and without wishing and compare.
Have a stranger do the flipping so nobody can tilt it.

flow.parent: Good answer: 7 heads in 10 happens by chance about one set in six, so it shows nothing yet. To be convincing she would need far more than half heads, over many more flips, compared with flips made without wishing. Her result is a reason to try more flips, not a proof.
flow.context: In this last step, you decide what the friend's 7 heads in 10 flips shows and what it does not.

experiments.title: Okra Pods: longer pods have more seeds. Which causes which?
experiments.context: In this experiment, you measure ten okra pods and count the seeds in each. You find a pattern, and then work out what the pattern can tell you and what it cannot.
experiments.question: Do longer okra pods have more seeds? And if they do, does that show that the seeds make the pod long?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will longer pods have more seeds? Will there be any exceptions? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We measure every pod from the stalk end to the tip with the same ruler. We cut open every pod in the same way and count every seed, including the small ones. We pick pods of different lengths, so that we can see the pattern. We count in the same way for every pod, and we write down the odd ones too.
results_table: Seeds for each centimetre (seeds divided by length)

materials.item: 10 okra pods (bhindi or vendakkai) of different lengths, from small to large
a ruler marked in centimetres
a table knife or a small kitchen knife, used only by a grown-up
a plate, a toothpick to move seeds while counting, and 10 small paper tags for the pod letters
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Cut on a board and keep the child's fingers away from the knife. Wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Measure the pods, cut them open, count the seeds, find the pattern and think about the cause.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then put the pods in a line from the shortest to the longest, and write the seed count under each. Circle any pod that does not fit the pattern.

flow.do: Show your child the ten pods. Ask for a guess about the pattern and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the page.
flow.say: Here are ten okra pods of different lengths. Do you think longer pods will have more seeds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Ten okra pods. Will longer pods have more seeds? Why?

ask.q: Why might a longer pod have more seeds?
good: It has more room.
It is older, so more seeds grew.
I do not know, we will count.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Okra Pods test. You guess before you count.

flow.do: Write the letters A to J on small paper tags. Put a tag by each pod. Your child measures each pod from stalk end to tip. Write the length to the nearest half centimetre.
flow.say: Give each pod a letter. Measure from the stalk end to the tip. Write the length in the table.
flow.kid: Give each pod a letter. Measure each pod. Write the length.
flow.parent: Choose pods of clearly different sizes, from about 5 centimetres to 14 centimetres. If the pods are all about the same size, the pattern will be hard to see.
flow.context: In this step, you measure each pod and write its length.

flow.do: A grown-up slits each pod open on a board. Your child counts the seeds with a toothpick, in groups of five. Write the number in the table.
flow.say: I will cut each pod open. You count the seeds. Move them in groups of five with the toothpick, so you do not lose count.
flow.kid: Count the seeds in each pod. Move them in fives. Write the number.
flow.wait: Counting takes about one minute a pod. Take a short break if your child tires.
flow.parent: Count every seed, even the tiny pale ones. A tender pod may have fewer and smaller seeds. If your child loses count, start that pod again. An honest recount is better than a guess.
flow.context: In this step, you cut open each pod and count the seeds.

flow.do: For each pod, divide the number of seeds by the length to get the seeds for each centimetre. Line up the pods from shortest to longest on the plate with the seed count under each. Look for the pattern and circle any odd pod.
flow.say: Put the pods in a line, from the shortest to the longest. What do you notice about the seeds? Which pod does not fit?
flow.kid: Line up the pods. Do longer pods have more seeds? Find an odd pod.

ask.q: What pattern do you see? Is there any pod that does not fit?
good: Longer pods have more seeds, mostly.
Pod F is long but has few seeds.
The seeds for each centimetre are about the same.

flow.parent: Most families see that longer pods have more seeds, with a few that do not fit. The seeds for each centimetre will often be close to each other. That is a strong pattern but it is not perfect, and the odd pod is worth talking about.
flow.context: In this step, you look for the pattern in your table.

flow.do: Read aloud the three stories below, which could each explain the pattern. Ask your child whether the table can tell which story is true. Then ask what test could.
flow.say: Story one: more seeds make the pod grow long. Story two: a long pod just has room for more seeds. Story three: something else, like how old the pod is, makes it long and full of seeds. Can our table tell us which is true?
flow.kid: Three stories explain the pattern. Can your table tell which is true?

check.q: In a table of okra pods, longer pods have more seeds. What does this show?
options: The seeds make the pod grow long
The pod and the seeds go together, but the table cannot say which makes which
The seeds and the length are not connected at all
check.why: The table shows a correlation. It cannot tell which causes which, or whether something else, such as the age of the pod, is behind both. A wrong pick usually means a pattern was read as a cause.

flow.parent: Scientists have tested a similar question in strawberries. When they removed the small seeds from one side of a growing strawberry, the fruit stopped growing on that side. That is an experiment, not just a pattern. A pattern points to where to look.
flow.context: In this last step, you think about what the okra pattern can and cannot tell you.

activities.title: Find the Third Thing in a Table
activities.context: In this activity, you read three small tables of made-up numbers. In each one, two things go together. You work out what is really going on: a hidden third thing, or the second thing causing the first.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
the three tables written out in the steps below, copied onto a page

schedule.what: Read each table, name the pattern, find the hidden third thing, and say how to check by comparing like with like.

activities.record: For each table, write what goes together, your guess for the hidden third thing, and one way you could check.

flow.do: Copy this table for your child. A shop in Chennai. January: 20 cold drinks and 2 fans. March: 90 and 11. May: 200 and 24. July: 150 and 17. October: 60 and 6. December: 15 and 1. Ask what goes together.
flow.say: This shop sold cold drinks and fans each month. Look at the numbers. What do you notice goes together?
flow.kid: A shop sold cold drinks and fans. What goes together in the numbers?

ask.q: What goes together in this table?
good: When cold drinks go up, fans go up too.
May is the biggest for both, and December is the smallest.

flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Third Thing. You read a table from a shop and spot what goes together.

flow.do: Ask your child if cold drinks make people buy fans. Ask what is different about May and December. Then read the question below.
flow.say: Does selling more cold drinks make people buy fans? What is different about May and December?
flow.kid: Do cold drinks make people buy fans? What is different in May?

check.q: A shop sells more cold drinks and more fans in the same months. What is the best explanation?
options: Cold drinks make people want fans
Hot weather makes people want both
Fans make people thirsty
check.why: The heat is a hidden third thing. It makes people thirsty and it makes people want fans. A wrong pick usually means the pattern was read as a cause, with no search for the third thing.

flow.parent: To check, compare like with like. Look only at the hot months, for example April, May and June. If cold drinks and fans still go up and down together within the hot months, there may be more to find. If they do not, the heat explains the pattern.
flow.context: In this step, you decide what is behind the shop's numbers.

flow.do: Copy the second table. A school, by class. Class 1: foot length 17 centimetres, spelling mark 4 out of 10. Class 2: 18.5 and 5. Class 3: 20 and 6. Class 4: 21.5 and 7. Class 5: 23 and 8. Ask for the hidden third thing.
flow.say: Children with longer feet get better spelling marks. Does a bigger foot help spelling? What is behind both? How could we check?
flow.kid: Longer feet, better spelling marks. What is behind both? How could you check?

ask.q: What is the hidden third thing here, and how could you check it?
good: Age. Older children have bigger feet and know more spelling.
Look only at children of the same age, and see if bigger feet still go with better spelling.

flow.parent: Comparing only children of the same age is the way to hold the third thing the same. Among children of one age, foot length and spelling mark do not go together. That is the check.
flow.context: In this step, you look at a school table and find the hidden third thing.

flow.do: Read the third example. A boy carried an umbrella on 4 of 6 days, and his school shoes were muddy on the same 4 days. Ask if the umbrella makes the shoes muddy, and which came first.
flow.say: A boy's umbrella days were also his muddy shoe days. Does the umbrella make shoes muddy? What came first? Now make up your own pair of things that go together, and say what is behind them.
flow.kid: Umbrella days were muddy shoe days. What is behind both? Make up your own pair.

check.q: A boy carried an umbrella on 4 of 6 days. His shoes were muddy on the same 4 days. What is the best explanation?
options: The umbrella made the ground muddy
Rain made him carry an umbrella and also made his shoes muddy
Muddy shoes make it rain
check.why: Rain is the hidden third thing. It leads to the umbrella and to the mud. A wrong pick usually means a child chose the first idea that linked the two things.

flow.context: In this step, you work out a third example and invent one of your own.

setup.art: A notebook page with a copied table of months, cold drinks and fans, and a child pointing at the row for May with a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Copy a table. Find what goes together.

setup.caption: 2. Draw an arrow from the hidden third thing to each column.

activities.title: The Fancy Label Cups: does a label change what we taste?
activities.context: In this activity, you pour the same drink into cups and give people two tastings. In the first, one cup has a fancy label. In the second, nobody knows which is which. You find out whether knowing the label changes what people say.

materials.item: a jug of squash or lemon water, made once and poured into every cup, so every cup holds exactly the same drink
16 small clean paper cups, four for each of 4 tasters (two cups in each round)
a coin
slips of paper: two with the words POSH SHOP and HOME-MADE, and two with the numbers 1 and 2
at least 4 people to taste: family, neighbours, or the same people twice on two days
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Use only a food-safe drink such as lemon water or squash. Ask each taster about allergies first. Every taster gets their own clean cup. Tell everybody the truth right after the test.

schedule.what: Make the drink, run the open tasting, run the blind tasting, reveal the trick, and count.

activities.record: A table with one row for each taster. Columns: Open tasting (which cup they said was better) and Blind tasting (which cup they said was better). At the bottom, count how many chose POSH SHOP in round 1 and how many chose cup 1 in round 2.

flow.do: A grown-up makes the squash in one jug. Your child writes four labels on slips of paper: POSH SHOP, HOME-MADE, 1 and 2. Ask for a guess and a reason before anyone tastes.
flow.say: We will taste two cups. One will be labelled posh shop, and one home-made. Do you think people will like the posh shop one more? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two cups, one labelled posh shop. Will people like it more? Why?

ask.q: Why might a label change what someone says they taste?
good: People think posh things must taste better.
It makes them expect a nicer taste.
It would not change anything, because the drink is the drink.

flow.parent: Do not tell your child the cups hold the same drink. Say only that you are testing what people say. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fancy Label Cups. You make the drink and guess what will happen.

flow.do: Round 1, open tasting. For each taster, fill two cups from the jug. Flip a coin. If it is heads, the left cup gets the POSH SHOP label. If it is tails, the right cup gets it. The other cup gets the HOME-MADE label. Ask which tastes better. Write the answer.
flow.say: Taste this cup and this cup. This one is from a posh shop, and this one is home-made. Which tastes better?
flow.kid: Flip the coin to decide the labels. Ask which tastes better. Write it down.
flow.parent: Say the same words to every taster. Do not look at the cups while they decide, because your face might give them a hint. Let the coin decide which side gets the label, so your own choice cannot tilt the test.
flow.context: In this step, you run the open tasting, with labels showing.

flow.do: Round 2, blind tasting. The taster looks away. Fill two fresh cups from the jug. Flip a coin to decide which cup gets the slip marked 1 and which gets the slip marked 2. Ask which tastes better. Write it down.
flow.say: Close your eyes while I put the numbers on. Now taste each cup. Which tastes better, one or two?
flow.kid: The taster looks away. Put the numbers 1 and 2 on the cups. Ask which tastes better.
flow.parent: In a double-blind version, a second person fills and labels the cups and the asker does not know either. If you can, try it. If you cannot, make a note that the asker knew.
flow.context: In this step, you run the blind tasting, with only numbers on the cups.

flow.do: Tell everyone the truth: both cups held the same drink. Then count how many picked POSH SHOP in round 1, and how many picked cup 1 in round 2.
flow.say: Both cups held exactly the same drink from one jug. Let's count. How many chose the posh shop cup? How many chose cup one?
flow.kid: Both cups had the same drink! Count how many picked the posh label and cup 1.
flow.parent: Be kind about the trick. Some tasters will say they really did taste a difference. That is interesting, and they are not lying. Expecting something can change what we notice.
flow.context: In this step, you tell everyone the truth and count the picks.

flow.do: Ask your child what the counts show. Ask whether it could be luck, with so few tasters. Ask what you could do to be surer.
flow.say: What does your count show? With only a few tasters, could it be luck? What would we do to be more sure?
flow.kid: What does your count show? Could it be luck? How could you be surer?

check.q: Most tasters picked the POSH SHOP cup in round 1. In round 2, about half picked cup 1. Both cups held the same drink. What does this suggest?
options: The label changed what people said
The posh drink really was better
People cannot taste anything
check.why: When nobody knew the labels, the picks were spread about evenly. When the label showed, more people picked it. That suggests the label changed what they said. With few tasters, chance could also play a part, so repeat with more people. A wrong pick usually means the child forgot that both cups were the same.

flow.parent: Studies of tasting have found that price and label can change what people report. In a home test with a handful of tasters, chance can hide the effect or make it look bigger. If your results differ, write them down as they are. That is also a useful result.
flow.context: In this last step, you decide what the counts show and how sure you can be.

setup.caption: 1. Round 1: two cups from one jug, one with a fancy label.
