activities.title: Same Numbers, Two Charts: does the starting line fool us?
activities.context: In this activity, you draw two bar charts of exactly the same two numbers. You show them to different people and see whether the way the chart is drawn changes what people say.

materials.item: squared paper or graph paper
a ruler and a pencil
coloured pencils
two people to show the charts to

schedule.what: Draw a chart that starts at zero, draw a chart that starts at 90, show them, and compare what people say.

activities.record: Keep your two charts. Under each one, write the answer each person gave to the question: how much better is Brand Two? The answer is a little, a bit, or much.

flow.do: Tell your child about two biscuit brands. In a crunch test, Brand One scored 92 out of 100 and Brand Two scored 95. Draw chart A with the side numbers from 0 to 100. Draw one bar for each brand.
flow.say: Two biscuit brands got crunch scores. Brand One scored ninety-two. Brand Two scored ninety-five. Draw a bar for each, with the side scale starting at zero.
flow.kid: Brand One scored 92. Brand Two scored 95. Draw two bars. Start the scale at 0.
flow.context: This is the first step of Same Numbers, Two Charts. You draw the first chart, starting at zero.
flow.parent: One square on the paper can stand for 5 points. The bars should look almost the same height.

flow.do: Draw chart B on a new page with the same two numbers. This time start the side scale at 90, so the side numbers run from 90 to 100. Draw one bar for each brand.
flow.say: Now draw the same two numbers again. This time the side scale starts at ninety. What do you notice about the bars?
flow.kid: Draw the same numbers again. Start the scale at 90 this time.

ask.q: How do the two bars look in chart B?
good: Brand Two's bar looks much taller.
One bar is tiny and the other is big.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the second chart of the same numbers, starting at 90.

flow.do: Show chart A to one person and chart B to another, or to the same person on another day. Cover the numbers. Ask: how much better is Brand Two? A little, a bit, or much? Write each answer.
flow.say: Look at this chart of biscuit crunch. How much better is Brand Two than Brand One? A little, a bit, or much?
flow.kid: Show each chart to a different person. Ask: how much better is Brand Two?
flow.parent: Say exactly the same words to both people. Keep the numbers on the side of the chart covered, so they judge only by how tall the bars look.
flow.context: In this step, you show each chart to a different person and ask the same question.

flow.do: Uncover the numbers. Talk about which chart is honest. Ask when it is fine to start a scale above zero.
flow.say: Both charts show the same numbers. Which one tells the truth about the difference? Is it ever fine to start the scale above zero?
flow.kid: Same numbers, different bars. Which chart is honest? Why?

check.q: Two bars show scores of 92 and 95. On chart B the scale starts at 90, and one bar looks about 2.5 times as tall as the other. What is the problem?
options: The numbers are wrong
The scale starts high, so a small gap looks huge
Chart B is too colourful
check.why: The scores are close. Starting the scale at 90 hides the part of the bar below 90, so a small difference looks big. A wrong pick usually means the child trusted the picture and not the numbers.

flow.parent: A scale that starts above zero can be fine for a line graph of temperature, if it is clearly labelled, because the interesting part is the change. For bars, which show amounts, it is safest to start at zero.
flow.context: In this last step, you uncover the numbers and decide which chart is honest.

setup.art: Two bar charts side by side on squared paper showing the same two scores, 92 and 95, one starting at 0 and one starting at 90.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the same two numbers on a chart that starts at 0 and on one that starts at 90.

setup.art: A boy showing one chart to his grandfather and the other chart to his sister, with the numbers covered by paper.
setup.caption: 2. Show each chart to a different person. Ask the same question.

projects.title: The Banana Test: does wrapping the stalk slow ripening?
projects.context: In this 6-day project, you test a kitchen saying: wrapping the stalk end of a banana slows its ripening. You use a coin to choose which bananas get wrapped, and you compare each wrapped banana with an unwrapped twin from the same bunch.

materials.item: a hand of 6 bananas from the same bunch, all about the same greenness
3 small squares of kitchen foil or cling film, each about 6 centimetres across, to wrap the stalk ends
a coin, to choose which banana in each pair is wrapped
6 paper tags and a pencil, to number the bananas 1 to 6
a tray or plate, and one shelf or table out of direct sun
a notebook, to draw the colour scale and the table

projects.safety: Bananas are food, so wash hands first. Fold the edges of the foil over, because cut foil can be sharp. Eat the bananas after the test, or share them.

schedule.what: Separate the bananas, number them, make pairs, flip coins, wrap, and set them on a tray.
Score the colour of each banana on the 1 to 5 scale.
Score the colour of each banana.
Score the colour of each banana.
Score the colour of each banana.
Score the colour, compare each pair, count, and decide what the test shows.

projects.record: A table with six rows (bananas 1 to 6) and columns for Pair, Wrapped or bare, and the colour score on each of days 1 to 6. At the end, a line for each pair that says which banana ripened faster, or that they tied.

flow.do: 1. Gently break a hand (a bunch) of 6 bananas into single bananas. Give each a tag, 1 to 6. 2. Make three pairs: 1 and 2, 3 and 4, 5 and 6. 3. For each pair, flip a coin. Heads, the first banana is wrapped. Tails, the second one is. 4. Wrap the stalk end of the chosen bananas in foil. 5. Lay all six on a tray in the same place. 6. Draw the colour scale on the page.
flow.say: People say wrapping the stalk makes bananas last longer. We will test it. First, guess. Will the wrapped bananas ripen slower, faster, or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Number the bananas. Make three pairs. Flip a coin for each pair. Wrap the chosen ones.

ask.q: Why do we use a coin to choose which banana is wrapped?
good: So I cannot pick the greener one by accident.
So it is fair.
Because I might wrap the one I think will last longer.

flow.parent: The colour scale: 1 is all green. 2 is green with a little yellow. 3 is mostly yellow with green tips. 4 is all yellow. 5 is yellow with brown spots. Do not tell your child what you expect. Results with only three pairs can be mixed, and that is an honest finding.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Banana Test. You make the pairs, flip the coins and wrap the bananas.

flow.do: Each morning at about the same time, your child scores each banana's colour on the 1 to 5 scale. Write it in the table. Do not move the bananas.
flow.say: Look at each banana. Which colour number is it today? Write it in the table. Do not move them around.
flow.kid: Score each banana from 1 to 5. Write it in the table.
flow.wait: Do this on days 2 to 5, about four minutes each day.
flow.parent: Score before you look at the tag, if you can, so what you expect does not change the score. A second person can score without knowing which are wrapped. That makes the test blind.
flow.context: In this step, you score the banana colours once a day.

flow.do: On day 6, score the bananas once more. For each pair, say which banana ripened faster, or that they tied. Count the pairs in which the wrapped banana ripened slower. Write what the test shows and what it cannot.
flow.say: Look at each pair. Which ripened faster? In how many pairs did the wrapped banana ripen slower? Is that enough to be sure?
flow.kid: Compare each pair. Count the pairs in which the wrapped banana ripened slower.

check.q: In a banana test, 2 of 3 wrapped bananas ripened slower than their twin. What is the fairest thing to say?
options: Wrapping the stalk definitely slows ripening
Two pairs out of three is too few to be sure, so repeat with more pairs
Wrapping makes no difference at all
check.why: Three pairs is a small number, and luck could easily give 2 out of 3. It is a hint to try again with more pairs. A wrong pick usually means a few tries were read as proof.

flow.parent: Whatever you find, report it as it is. If the wrapped bananas ripened slower in all three pairs, repeat with a new hand to see if it holds. If they tied or the bare ones were slower, say so. Ripening depends on temperature and on how ripe the fruit was when picked.
flow.context: In this last step, you compare the pairs and decide what the test shows.

setup.caption: 1. Make three pairs. Let a coin decide which banana is wrapped.

setup.art: A child holding a banana next to a hand-drawn colour scale from 1 (green) to 5 (yellow with spots) and writing in a table.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, score every banana on the colour scale.

challenges.title: The Honest Report: say what your evidence shows, and no more
challenges.problem: Use the numbers from one of your own tests: the coin, the okra pods or the bananas. Make a one-page report that tells a family what you found, and clearly says what you cannot say.
constraints: The report has four boxes: What we did, What we saw, What we can say, What we cannot say.
Each box has at most 40 words.
At least one real number from your table must appear.
Box four must give one way you could be wrong and one test to do next.
materials: your results table from one of the tests
a second person to read your report
general: Box one: say what you did so another family could repeat it, with the amounts and the number of tries.
Box two: give your numbers and draw your bar chart.
Box three: use careful words such as 'in our test' and 'about'.
Box four: say what you cannot say, one reason you might be wrong, and one test for next time.
creative: Colour the boxes like a traffic light: green for what we saw, amber for what we think, red for what we cannot say.
Draw a confidence meter like a thermometer with low, medium and high, and mark how sure you are.
Ask a friend to find the weakest sentence in your report, and rewrite it so that it says no more than the numbers show.
challenges.your_turn: Swap reports with a friend or a parent. Ask the three questions: Says who? How do they know? What is missing? Then fix your report.

flow.do: Read this report aloud: 'Our test proves that okra seeds make pods grow long. Everyone knows seeds make fruit big.' Ask your child what is wrong with it.
flow.say: Here is a report: 'Our test proves that okra seeds make pods grow long. Everyone knows seeds make fruit big.' What is wrong with it?
flow.kid: This report says seeds make pods long. What is wrong with it?

ask.q: What is wrong with this report?
good: It says proves, but the table only shows the seeds and length go together.
It says everyone knows, but that is not evidence.
It does not say how many pods.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Honest Report challenge. You find what is wrong with a careless report.

flow.do: Your child writes the four boxes for their own test. Check that each box has at most 40 words and that box four names one risk and one next test.
flow.say: Write your four boxes. Keep each box short. In the last box, say what you cannot say.
flow.kid: Write the four boxes. Use real numbers. Say what you cannot say.
flow.parent: Strong reports use words like 'in our test', 'about' and 'might'. If your child says 'proves', ask what else could explain the numbers.
flow.context: In this step, you write the report.

flow.do: Swap reports with another person. They read it and ask: says who, how do they know, and what is missing? Your child fixes the weakest sentence.
flow.say: Read your friend's report. Ask the three questions. Is there a sentence that says more than the numbers show?
flow.kid: Read a friend's report. Ask the three questions. Fix the weakest sentence.

check.q: A report says: Our coin test proves that coins land heads more than tails. 108 of 200 flips were heads. What is the best fix?
options: Say 'in our test, 108 of 200 flips were heads, which could be chance'
Delete the numbers
Say 'everyone knows coins prefer heads'
check.why: 108 heads out of 200 is close to half, and chance alone often gives this. The honest report gives the numbers and says it could be chance. A wrong pick usually means a child wants the report to sound bigger than the evidence.

flow.context: In this last step, you swap reports and fix the weakest sentence.

items.p: Two things that rise and fall together are said to have a ____.
items.why: A correlation is a real pattern, but it does not say what causes what.

items.p: In Pune, the months when more woollen shawls are sold are also the months when more hot tea is sold. What is the best explanation?
opts: Cold weather makes people want both
Shop owners plan it that way
items.why: The cold weather is a hidden third thing. It makes people reach for a shawl and a hot cup. The shawls and the tea never touch each other.

items.p: True or false: if two things go together, one of them must cause the other.
items.why: False. Two things can go together because a hidden third thing is behind both, because the arrow points the other way, or by chance.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: Something outside the table that pushes both things up and down
The group treated the same, except it does not get the thing being tested
A dummy treatment with nothing active in it
People do not know which group they are in
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four ideas are the tools for testing a pattern fairly.

items.p: Sort each pattern: is there a hidden third thing, or does the arrow point the other way?
items: Patients who stay longer in hospital are sicker.
Cities with more bridges have more boats.
Rooms with an air cooler feel hotter than rooms without one.
Towns with more schools have more stationery shops.
People who use walking sticks have had more falls.
Months with more school bags sold also have more uniforms sold.
items.a: see items
items.why: Sicker people stay longer, hot rooms get coolers, and falls lead to sticks. Rivers, town size and the start of the school year are the hidden third things.

items.p: A fair coin is flipped 10 times and gives 8 heads. What is the best thing to say?
opts: This can happen by chance, so flip many more times before deciding
items.why: About 1 set of 10 in 18 gives 8 or more heads from chance alone. Ten flips is too few to decide. The way to find out is to flip many more times.

items.p: In The Lucky Coin experiment, the total of all 200 flips is closer to half than most single sets of 10. Explain why.
items.a: A strong answer says that in a small set luck can swing far from half, but over many flips the highs and lows cancel out, so the total settles near half.
items.why: A strong answer connects more tries with steadier results.

items.p: The group that is treated the same as the others, but does not get the thing being tested, is called the ____ group.
items.why: You compare the test group with the control group to see what the thing really does.

items.p: In a double-blind test of a medicine, who does not know who got the real medicine?
opts: Both the patients and the people handing out and measuring
items.why: If either side knows, a look, a word or a hope could change what is reported. When neither side knows, that cannot happen.

items.p: True or false: when people in a test feel better after a dummy pill, the feeling is real, but the pill did not cure anything.
items.why: True. In many tests, people report real changes after a placebo, especially in pain. A sugar pill cannot kill germs or heal bones.

items.p: Children who wear sandals more often catch fewer colds. Name a hidden third thing and say how you would check it.
items.a: A strong answer names the season, for example warm weather: children wear sandals in hot months, and fewer colds go round in hot months. To check, compare only children in the same month and see if sandals still go with fewer colds.
items.why: A strong answer finds a third thing and checks by comparing like with like.

items.p: Draw a diagram with three circles. Show a hidden third thing with an arrow to each of two things that go together. Use the golas and sunburn on the beach, or your own example.
items.a: A sun circle with arrows to a gola circle and a sunburn circle, and a dotted line with a cross between the gola and the sunburn.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the hidden third thing on top with arrows down, and shows no direct arrow between the other two.
items.art: A blank page with three empty circles arranged as a triangle.

items.p: Look at this bar chart of two biscuit scores. Label the part that makes the gap look bigger than it is, and say where the scale should start.
items.a: Label the side scale that starts at 90, and say that it should start at 0.
items.why: A scale that starts at 90 cuts off the bottom of both bars, so a small gap looks big.
items.art: A bar chart of two bars with the side scale beginning at 90 and a blank label box by the scale.

items.p: Why do we use a coin flip to choose which banana in a pair gets wrapped?
opts: So the choice does not depend on what the tester hopes
items.why: If the tester picks, they may wrap the greener banana without knowing. A coin has no favourites, so the two groups come out alike.

items.p: Two cousins in Madurai argue about a herbal tea.

views.says: My aunt drank the tea and her cold was gone in a week. The tea works.
Colds go away in a week anyway. We would have to compare people who drank it with people who did not.

items.ask: Which cousin do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other cousin has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that one story cannot show what would have happened without the tea. It also gives Janani her due: her aunt's experience is real and a good reason to run a fair test.
items.why: Marks go for using the idea of a control group and for being fair to the other cousin.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair comparison in order.
items: Flip a coin to decide which one gets the treatment
Write down the results every time
Pick similar items from the same batch
Treat both groups the same except for one thing
a: Pick similar items from the same batch
Flip a coin to decide which one gets the treatment
Treat both groups the same except for one thing
Write down the results every time
items.why: You start with alike things, let chance split them, change only one thing, record, and then compare.

items.p: A plant food is tested on 6 plants. The tester gives it to the 3 tallest plants. Why is this a problem?
opts: The tester may have chosen the strongest plants, so any difference may not come from the food
items.why: If the tester chooses, the strongest plants may grow best whatever they are fed. A coin flip would have made the two groups alike.

items.p: A newspaper says: children who eat breakfast do better in school. Give a possible hidden third thing, and say how the arrow could go the other way.
items.a: A strong answer names a third thing such as family money, a calm morning at home or sleep. For the other way round, children who feel well and do well at school may be more likely to get up and eat.
items.why: A strong answer looks for a third thing and for the opposite arrow.

items.p: One doctor tries a tonic on 5 people, and 4 feel better. Another doctor tries it on 5,000 people. Half get the tonic and half get a dummy. With the tonic, 52 in 100 feel better. With the dummy, 50 in 100 feel better. Which is stronger evidence for the tonic?
opts: The first, because 4 out of 5 is a bigger share
The second, because it has many people and a comparison group
The first, because it is quicker
items.why: The second test is large and has a control group. It shows only a tiny gap. The first has too few people and no comparison.

items.p: True or false: a poll that asks one million people is always right.
items.why: False. If the million people are not like everyone, the answer is still wrong. A big sample cannot fix asking the wrong people.

items.p: A dummy pill with nothing active in it, used in a test, is called a ____.
items.why: A placebo lets testers separate the effect of the real treatment from the effect of expecting to feel better.

items.p: Sort each test: does it have a fair comparison, or is a control group missing?
items: Someone wrapped three bananas and watched them ripen.
Someone wrapped three bananas and left three twins bare, and a coin chose which got wrapped.
Someone gave a new tonic to a whole class and they all felt fine.
A coin split the class in two. One half used a new spelling game and the other kept the old way. Both did the same test.
items.a: see items
items.why: Without a group that did not get the treatment, we cannot tell what would have happened anyway.

items.p: Seven heads in 10 flips is not strong evidence of anything, but 70 heads in 100 flips would be. Explain the difference.
items.a: A strong answer says that with 10 flips, luck often gives 7 heads, about 1 set in 6. With 100 flips, an ordinary coin almost never gives 70 or more heads, so it would be a surprise and would be worth looking into.
items.why: A strong answer says that a result is a surprise only when chance rarely gives it.

items.p: John Snow's comparison of houses supplied by two water companies on the same streets was strong evidence. Why?
opts: The houses were the same in most ways except the water
items.why: Because neighbours on the same streets shared the air, the poverty and the weather, the main difference left was the water. That cut out many hidden third things.

items.p: Match each sneaky trick to an example.
pairs: Showing three happy customers and hiding three hundred who complained
Testing a toothpaste on four people
Handing out a survey at a biscuit stall
A label with long words and no named study
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each trick leaves out something you need to judge the claim.

items.p: Three of these make evidence stronger. Which is the odd one out?
opts: The seller of the product ran the test
items.why: A seller gains from one answer, so a test run only by the seller is weaker. The other three make evidence stronger.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi talk about a headache tablet test.

views.says: People in the test felt better after the sugar pill, so they were only pretending. Placebo means fake.
The feeling can be real, because expecting to feel better can change how we feel. But a sugar pill cannot fix a broken bone.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer sees that placebo effects are real feelings, especially for pain, but do not cure everything. It gives Rohit his due: a sugar pill has nothing in it that acts like a medicine.
items.why: Marks go for using evidence and stating the other view fairly.

items.p: A friend says playing music helps bean seeds sprout faster. Draw a fair test with two trays, a coin, and what stays the same.
items.a: Two trays with the same beans, same water, same light and same warmth. A coin decides which seeds go to which tray. Only one tray has music.
items.why: A strong drawing changes one thing, keeps the rest the same and lets a coin choose.
items.art: Two empty trays side by side, an empty coin box and a blank space for a list headed Stays the same.

items.p: Here is a results table from the Okra Pods experiment. Label the column that was measured, the column that was counted, and the column that was worked out.
items.a: Length is measured. Seeds is counted. Seeds for each centimetre is worked out.
items.why: Measuring uses a ruler, counting uses your eyes and fingers, and the last column uses arithmetic on the first two.
items.art: A table with columns Pod, Length in centimetres, Number of seeds, Seeds for each centimetre, and three empty label boxes above.

items.p: In the Okra Pods experiment, longer pods had more seeds. Give two different stories that could explain this, other than that seeds make pods long.
items.a: A strong answer might say that a longer pod has more room for seeds, or that older pods have had more time to grow both long and full of seeds.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a pattern can fit several stories until a further test decides.

items.p: In the Fancy Label Cups activity, every cup was filled from one jug. Why?
opts: So the drink is exactly the same, and only the label differs
So the jug would be empty sooner
items.why: If the drinks differed, a taste difference could come from the drink and not the label. Keeping the drink the same means any difference in picks comes from the label.

items.p: True or false: a chart that starts its scale at 90 shows different numbers from one that starts at 0.
items.why: False. The numbers are the same. Only the picture changes, which is why it is wise to read the numbers on the side.

items.p: A shop owner says: Our own test proved that our oil is the healthiest. What three questions would you ask?
items.a: A strong answer asks who ran the test, how many people took part and what was compared with what, and whether anyone else has repeated it.
items.why: A strong answer asks about the source, the method and who is missing.

items.p: A friend says tying a red thread to a tulsi plant makes her grow faster. Plan a fair test. Say how many plants, what the control is, how a coin is used, what stays the same, and what you record.
items.a: A strong plan uses several tulsi pots of the same size and age, a coin to choose which get a red thread, the same water, soil and light for all, and measures the height of each plant on the same days. The pots without a thread are the control.
items.why: A strong plan includes a control, random choice, fairness and a clear record.

items.p: A school tries a new reading method on its best readers and compares them with last year's class. What is the main problem?
opts: The two groups were different from the start
The best readers are too few
Last year is too long ago
items.why: The best readers were already ahead, and last year's children may differ in other ways. A coin should split a single class into two groups.

items.p: Three people talk about John Snow and the cholera pump in 1854.

views.says: Snow's map proved the water was the cause. The deaths were all around the pump.
The map only showed a pattern. The comparison of houses on the same streets with different water made it strong.
Both mattered. The map showed where to look, and the comparison tested whether the water was the cause.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Can more than one be right? Explain.
items.a: A strong answer sees that a map shows a pattern, and a comparison of like with like tests a cause. Charu's view joins the other two, though Anand overstates what a map alone can prove.
items.why: Marks go for reasons and for being fair to the other views.

items.p: Sort each question: could you settle it with a home experiment, or do you need another kind of evidence?
items: Does salt make a potato float?
What made the dinosaurs die out?
Was the Sun dimmer a million years ago?
Does music help bean seeds sprout?
Why did a city have a cholera outbreak in 1854?
items.a: see items
items.why: We can run tests on things we can reach and change. For the past or the very far away, scientists compare the best records they have.

items.p: An advert says: In a test, 8 out of 10 athletes ran faster after our drink. What is the main thing missing?
opts: A group of athletes who ran without the drink
items.why: Athletes often run faster the second time, because of warm-up and practice. Without a group that did not get the drink, we cannot tell what the drink did.

items.p: Children who sleep with the light on are more afraid of the dark. Say how the arrow could go the other way, and how you could find out which came first.
items.a: A strong answer says that children who are afraid of the dark may ask for the light to be left on. To find out which came first, ask parents when the fear began and when the light started to stay on.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the fear may have come first and led to the light being left on.

items.p: Two teams in different cities use different groups of people and find the same result. Is that stronger evidence than one team getting the same result twice?
items.why: True. If different people in different places agree, a hidden problem in one place is unlikely to have fooled everybody.

items.p: Match each problem with its fix.
pairs: Tasters know which cup is posh
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each fix removes one way the evidence could be tilted.

items.p: In 200 coin flips, about how many times might you expect a run of four heads in a row to turn up?
opts: Only if the coin is bent
items.why: Each flip is a possible start of a run. Four heads in a row has a chance of 1 in 16 from any start. With about 197 starts, that is about 12 runs. A fair coin does this without any help.

items.p: Children who have more books at home do better at school. Draw a diagram with one or two hidden third things behind both.
items.a: Circles for books at home and school marks, with arrows from a third circle such as parents who read, family money or time at home, to both.
items.why: A strong diagram puts a third thing behind the pair and does not draw an arrow from books to marks.
items.art: A blank page with two circles labelled Books at home and School marks, and space above for a third circle.

items.p: Should we act on a pattern before we know its cause? Give an example when you would and an example when you would wait.
items.a: A strong answer says that we can act on a pattern when acting is cheap and safe, such as carrying an umbrella when clouds are dark. We should wait when acting is costly or could harm, such as banning a food or giving a medicine to children.
items.why: There is no one right answer. Marks go for weighing cost and risk against how strong the evidence is.

items.p: Here is a short test report. Label the part that says what was done, the part that says what was seen, and the part that says what cannot be said.
items.a: Label 'We flipped a coin 200 times' as what was done, '108 heads' as what was seen, and 'this could be chance' as what cannot be said.
items.why: An honest report keeps these three parts apart.
items.art: A short report with three lines: We flipped a coin 200 times. 108 were heads. This could be chance. Three empty label boxes sit beside the lines.

items.p: Put these in order, from the weakest evidence to the strongest.
items: A group chosen by a coin, with nobody knowing who got what
A comparison with a control group
a: A comparison with a control group
A group chosen by a coin, with nobody knowing who got what
items.why: Each step removes another way to be fooled, and agreement from many tests removes the most.

items.p: A review finds that studies paid for by makers of a drug more often favoured the drug. What should a careful reader do?
opts: Ask who paid for the study and look for independent tests that agree
items.why: Who paid does not prove a study is wrong, but it is a reason to look for other tests by people who gain nothing from the answer.

items.p: Villages with more tractors have bigger rice harvests. Give a hidden third thing, and a way the arrow might go the other way.
items.a: A strong answer might say that villages with good irrigation or rich soil have big harvests and can also afford tractors. For the other way round, a big harvest brings money that buys tractors.
items.why: A strong answer finds both a third thing and the reverse arrow.

items.p: Describe an advert or a claim you have seen at home or at school that used one of the sneaky tricks. Name the trick and say what you would ask.
items.a: A strong answer names a real claim, names the right trick, such as too few, only the hits or asked only fans, and gives a question that would find the missing piece.
items.why: This uses the ideas on something from the child's own life.

quiz.p: What does a correlation tell you about two things?
opts: That they rise and fall together, but not why
That they are the same thing
That one is bigger than the other
quiz.why: A correlation is a real pattern. It is a clue about where to look. It does not say what causes what.

quiz.p: In Chennai, on days when more people carry umbrellas, auto fares are higher. What is the best explanation?
opts: Rain makes people carry umbrellas and also makes autos harder to find
quiz.why: Rain is the hidden third thing behind both. People open umbrellas in rain, and autos are in demand in rain.

quiz.p: A girl suspects that the hot sun is behind a pattern between golas and sunburn. She compares only sunny days. Why does this help?
opts: On sunny days the sun is the same in every row, so she can see if golas still matter
The doctor works only on sunny days
quiz.why: Comparing like with like holds the hidden third thing the same. If golas and sunburn no longer go together among sunny days, the sun explains the pattern.

quiz.p: A fair coin is flipped 10 times and gives 7 heads. Which is the best conclusion?
opts: This happens by chance about 1 set in 6, so it shows very little
quiz.why: Seven or more heads in 10 flips comes up about 17 times in 100 sets from chance alone. It is too common to be a surprise.

quiz.p: Why does a total of 200 flips give a steadier picture than one set of 10 flips?
opts: Because over many flips the luck of single sets cancels out
quiz.why: In a small set, chance can swing far from half. In a large number of flips, the highs and lows balance out and the total settles near half.

quiz.p: Which is the best plan for testing whether wrapping a banana stalk slows ripening?
opts: Wrap one banana and watch it
Ask a neighbour what they think
Wrap three bananas and leave three twins bare, using a coin to choose, and score all six each day
Wrap all the bananas in the shop
quiz.why: You need twins from the same bunch, a control group left bare, and a coin to choose. That makes the two groups alike apart from the wrapping.

quiz.p: In a taste test, a coin decides which cup gets the fancy label. Why use a coin and not choose yourself?
opts: Your own choice could tilt the test without you noticing
The label looks nicer on one side
quiz.why: If you choose, you may put the label on the cup you expect people to like. A coin has no preference, so the label goes on either side by chance.

quiz.p: A medicine test gives half the people a sugar pill that looks identical to the real one. Why?
opts: So the effect of expecting to feel better can be told apart from the effect of the medicine
quiz.why: Both groups expect to feel better. If the medicine group improves more than the sugar pill group, the extra is the effect of the medicine.

quiz.p: In a double-blind test, who does not know which people got the real treatment?
opts: The people being tested and the people measuring
Only the scientist who designed it
quiz.why: If the testers know, a look or a word can give it away, and their hopes can change what they measure. When neither group knows, this cannot happen.

quiz.p: What is the most important thing to check on a bar chart before you trust the size of the gap?
opts: Whether the side scale starts at zero
quiz.why: If the scale starts above zero, the bottoms of the bars are cut off and a small gap can look large. The numbers on the side tell the truth.

quiz.p: A company says: Our own test shows our oil is the healthiest. What is the best next question?
opts: Has anyone else tested it, and who paid for the test?
quiz.why: A company gains if the answer is yes. Tests by others who gain nothing are stronger evidence.

quiz.p: In 1854, John Snow compared houses on the same streets that got water from two different companies. Why was this such strong evidence?
opts: The houses were alike in most ways except the water
quiz.why: The streets, the air and the poverty were the same. The main difference left was the water, so the difference in illness pointed to the water.

Health workers map where an illness is spreading and compare the people who fall ill with those who do not.
Farmers and agriculture colleges try a new seed on half the field and keep the other half as it was.
Weather scientists check forecasts against what happened over many years before they trust a method.
Engineers test a new bridge design against an old one under the same loads.
Teachers and schools compare two ways of teaching with a coin flip deciding who gets which.
Journalists ask who paid for a study and who was left out before they report it.
Judges and police look for other evidence because one witness can be sure and wrong.
Shoppers can spot an advert that shows only the happy customers.
Anyone can ask of a pattern in the news: what else changed on those days?

open_questions.q: Why do people see patterns in things that are random, such as faces in clouds and streaks in coins?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have ideas about how the brain is built to look for patterns, but nobody knows exactly why the habit is so strong or when it helps and when it fools us.

open_questions.q: How does expecting to feel better change what the body does?
open_questions.why_open: The placebo effect is real in many tests, especially for pain, but how it works is still being studied, and scientists disagree on how much it does.

open_questions.q: Can we ever be certain that one thing causes another?
open_questions.why_open: Philosophers from David Hume onwards have argued that we only ever see one thing follow another. Scientists use careful tests to get as close to certain as they can, but the argument is not over.

open_questions.q: How should a town act when the evidence is weak but the danger is serious?
open_questions.why_open: In London in 1854, the handle of the Broad Street water pump was taken off because of a strong hint that its water was spreading cholera, before the proof was complete. People still argue about how much evidence is enough before acting.

open_questions.q: Does a bigger test always mean a better test?
open_questions.why_open: Bigger tests are steadier, but they cost more, and a big test of the wrong people can still mislead. Scientists keep arguing about how to balance size and care.

open_questions.q: Which stories do we keep telling because they are true, and which because we like them?
open_questions.why_open: Historians and scientists are still sorting some well-known stories into what happened and what was added later. Nobody has checked every story.

Is this a pattern, a cause or a lucky streak?

jokes.a: He always opened on its busiest days.

jokes.j: What did the coin say after landing heads five times in a row?
jokes.a: Don't look at me. I'm only following chance.

jokes.j: What do you call a test with no control group?

jokes.j: Why did the bar chart start at 90?
What did one cup say to the other in the taste test?
jokes.a: We are exactly the same, but nobody believes us.

jokes.j: Why did the advert only show the winners?
jokes.a: The others were too shy to come to the photo.

jokes.j: Why did the detective love the beach?

jokes.j: Why did the okra pod win the counting contest?
jokes.a: Everyone could count on the pod.

jokes.j: Why did the banana bring a coin to the test?
jokes.a: Heads or tails is fairer than picking favourites.

maths.problem: In a Lucky Coin test, 4 of the 20 sets had 7 or more heads. What fraction of the sets is that, and what is it as a percent? Chance alone gives about 17 in 100 sets. Is the result close?
maths.answer: 4 out of 20 is one fifth, which is 20 percent. That is close to 17 percent.
maths.explain: 4 out of 20 is 4 divided by 20, which is 0.2, or 20 out of 100. That is 20 percent. Chance gives about 17 percent, so 20 percent is close. With only 20 sets, a few sets either way is normal.
maths.context: In the Lucky Coin test, you flip a coin in 20 sets of 10 and count how many sets give 7 or more heads.
maths.why_maths: A fraction or a percent lets you compare your count with how often chance is expected to do it.

maths.problem: One person got 7 heads in 10 flips. Another person got 103 heads in 200 flips. Write each as a percent of heads. Which result is closer to half?
maths.answer: The 10 flips: 70 percent. The 200 flips: 51.5 percent. The 200 flips are much closer to half.
maths.explain: 7 out of 10 is 70 out of 100, so 70 percent. 103 out of 200 is 51.5 out of 100, so 51.5 percent. Half is 50 percent. 70 is 20 away from 50, and 51.5 is only 1.5 away. More flips pull the result close to half.
maths.context: In the Lucky Coin test, you compare a short run of flips with a long one.
maths.why_maths: Turning both counts into percents lets you compare a small number of flips with a large number fairly.

maths.problem: A run of four heads in a row has a chance of 1 in 16 from any starting flip, because one half times one half times one half times one half is one sixteenth. In 200 flips there are about 197 places a run could start. About how many runs of four heads should a fair coin make?
maths.explain: 197 divided by 16 is about 12. So a fair coin is expected to make a dozen or so runs of four heads in 200 flips, with no wishing at all. Seeing one or two streaks is not a surprise.
maths.context: In the Lucky Coin test, you look for the longest streak of one side in your flips.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the number of starting places by the chance tells you how often a streak should turn up from luck alone.

maths.problem: In an okra test, a pod 8 centimetres long had 36 seeds, and a pod 12 centimetres long had 60 seeds. How many seeds is that for each centimetre in each pod? About how many seeds would you guess for a pod 10 centimetres long?
maths.answer: 4.5 seeds for each centimetre in the first pod, and 5 in the second. About 45 to 50 seeds for a pod of 10 centimetres.
maths.explain: 36 divided by 8 is 4.5. 60 divided by 12 is 5. A 10 centimetre pod lies between the two, so 10 times 4.5 is 45 and 10 times 5 is 50. We can guess between 45 and 50. A real pod might still be an odd one.
maths.context: In the Okra Pods test, you count the seeds in pods of different lengths.
maths.why_maths: Seeds for each centimetre turns two different pods into one comparable number, and lets you guess for a pod you have not opened.

maths.problem: On the beach, the sunburn cases on the five sunny days were 13, 15, 14, 14 and 14. On the two cloudy days they were 1 and 2. What is the average on sunny days and on cloudy days? About how many times as many cases are there on a sunny day?
maths.answer: Sunny days: 14. Cloudy days: 1.5. About 9 times as many.
maths.explain: 13 + 15 + 14 + 14 + 14 is 70, and 70 divided by 5 is 14. 1 + 2 is 3, and 3 divided by 2 is 1.5. 14 divided by 1.5 is about 9. So sunny days had about 9 times as many cases. The sun is the thing that changes the number of burns.
maths.context: This is about the story The Ban on the Gola Cart, where a girl compares sunny and cloudy days on a beach.
maths.why_maths: An average shows what a typical sunny day and a typical cloudy day look like, so you can see which thing really changes the number of burns.

maths.problem: Among the sunny days on the beach, one day had 120 golas and 14 sunburn cases. Another sunny day had no golas and 14 cases. How many more golas were sold on the first day? How many more sunburn cases? What does that say about golas?
maths.answer: 120 more golas and 0 more cases. Golas do not change the sunburn on sunny days.
maths.explain: 120 minus 0 is 120 more golas. 14 minus 14 is 0 more cases. So 120 extra golas brought no extra burns. If golas caused burns, the day with the most golas should have had more.
maths.context: This is about the story The Ban on the Gola Cart, where a girl looks only at sunny days.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the numbers for two days that are alike in one way shows whether the other thing made any difference.

maths.problem: On a street in a city, 20 houses used pump A and 20 houses used pump B. 6 houses using pump A and 1 house using pump B had an outbreak of illness. How many times as many houses with illness used pump A? Is that enough to be sure that pump A is the cause?
maths.answer: 6 times as many. It is a strong hint but 20 houses each is small, so check with more houses.
maths.explain: 6 divided by 1 is 6, so six times as many houses. With only 20 houses in each group, luck could play a part. A strong hint is a reason to test further, and also a reason to act with care while testing.
maths.context: This is about John Snow's comparison of houses with different water, using smaller made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: Comparing counts in two similar groups is how a natural experiment points to a cause, and the size of the groups tells you how far to trust it.

maths.problem: On a chart that starts at 0, with 1 centimetre for each 10 points, bars for scores of 92 and 95 are 9.2 and 9.5 centimetres tall. On a chart that starts at 90, with 1 centimetre for each point, how tall are the two bars? How many times taller is the second bar?
maths.answer: 2 centimetres and 5 centimetres. The second bar is 2.5 times taller.
maths.explain: On the second chart, 92 minus 90 is 2, so the first bar is 2 centimetres. 95 minus 90 is 5, so the second bar is 5 centimetres. 5 divided by 2 is 2.5. A gap of only 3 points looks like a bar two and a half times as tall.
maths.context: In the activity Same Numbers, Two Charts, you draw the same scores with two different starting lines.
maths.why_maths: Working out the bar heights shows how the starting line changes the picture even though the numbers stay the same.

roots.context: In the story The Ban on the Gola Cart, golas and sunburn went together because the hot sun was behind both. Now we ask what this tells us about how things in the world are connected.

deep_truth.truth: In the story The Ban on the Gola Cart, golas and sunburn rose and fell together, yet neither made the other happen. The hot sun was behind both, and it was not in the table. Many things that move together are two results of one hidden thing. Finding that thing is how we start to understand what is really going on.
deep_truth.habit: When we see two things together, we tend to decide that one causes the other. Usually we pick the one we noticed first as the cause of the one we care about. This feels like something we saw, but it is a guess, and it leaves out anything that may be behind both.
deep_truth.evidence: In the beach table from the story, golas no longer went with sunburn once only sunny days were compared, and a day with no golas still had burns. The Lucky Coin experiment shows that results jump around by luck alone. The Okra Pods experiment shows that a real pattern, longer pods with more seeds, still does not say what causes what.

three.who_am_i: You feel hot, thirsty and grumpy, all at the same time. You may blame one feeling for another. Often one thing, the heat, is behind all three.
three.what_is_life: Many flowers open when the sun is high, and bees come to them at that hour. Both the flowers and the bees are responding to the same sun.
three.what_is_this_world: Rain clouds, wet roads, open umbrellas and calling frogs all arrive together in the monsoon. They look like separate events, but many of them share one source.

roots.thread: When two things go together, there is always a reason. Sometimes one makes the other. Sometimes the second makes the first. Sometimes luck brings them together. And sometimes a third thing, like the sun, is behind both. Telling these apart takes patience, a fair comparison, and a willingness to look past what everyone has already noticed.

teachings.source: Samyutta Nikaya 12 (dependent origination), a collection of the Buddha's teachings
teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught: when this exists, that comes to be. When this does not exist, that does not come to be. Nothing arises alone. It arises from conditions.
teachings.link: In the story The Ban on the Gola Cart, there were no golas on the day the cart was closed, but people still got sunburnt. By the Buddha's test, the sunburn did not depend on the golas. It depended on the sun.

practice.say: Sit by a window. Feel the warmth on your arm. Look at the bright patch of light on the floor. Breathe in slowly three times. Now ask what is behind both the warmth and the light. Notice that it is one thing, far away, reaching both places at once.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1854, cholera struck the Soho part of London. Many doctors believed it spread through bad air, which they called miasma. A doctor named John Snow thought it spread through water. He marked each death on a map of the streets, and the marks gathered around one water pump on Broad Street. Then he looked for the exceptions. A workhouse near the pump, which had its own well, had few deaths. A brewery close by, where workers drank beer, had few or none. Some people far away who had water brought from the Broad Street pump fell ill. Snow also compared houses on the same streets that were supplied by two different water companies. The houses with the dirtier water had many times more deaths. The pump handle was taken off. A pattern was not enough for Snow. He looked for what stood behind it, and he checked by comparing like with like.
how_we_found_out.who: John Snow, an English doctor in London
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many doctors and officials believed that cholera was spread by bad air, called miasma. Snow's map, his search for the exceptions and his comparison of houses on the same streets showed that the water was carrying the illness.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Lucky Coin needs only a coin, a plate and a second person to write; the 20 sets take about 15 minutes, and the numbers in the unit (7 or more heads in 10 flips is 176 out of 1024, about 17 percent; a run of at least four of one side appears in about 46 percent of sets of ten) were counted exactly. Okra Pods works best with pods of clearly different lengths; a grown-up cuts them and counting is done in fives with a toothpick. The Fancy Label Cups uses one jug and a coin; with few tasters the open round may show no effect, and the steps say so. The Banana Test has only three pairs, so the result is honestly shaky and the steps say so; ripening depends on temperature. To verify before publishing: the details of John Snow's workhouse and brewery (reported as few or no deaths), the 1936 poll (more than two million replies), the strawberry seed result (Nitsch, 1950), the birthday figure (about 7 in 10 for 30 children), and the three videos, whose YouTube addresses are still to be found. The spine (intro, Find the Third Thing, The Lucky Coin, the explanation cards, how we found out, roots and quiz) fits about 100 minutes in two sessions.
